newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil market waits for taste of Iraq's oil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil market waits for taste of Iraq's oil.

text.p: World crude oil prices weakened on Monday after the United Nations cleared the first Iraqi crude oil exports forbidden to the market for nearly six years, but the reaction was measured.

Benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea fell to $23.95 a barrel before recovering to $24.06 a barrel, down 48 cents, after U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali gave final approval to the partial Iraqi oil sales deal.
Crude oil prices remain around $3.0 a barrel higher than this time last year, largely because of the absence of some three million barrels of Iraqi crude oil.

Even Monday's 50 cent drop was merely a reversal of a sharp rally on Friday, traders remarked. They said the market's immediate reaction was psychological and they remained sceptical any Iraqi oil will be seen on the world market for several weeks yet.

"The Iraqis have been threatening us with their sword of Damocles for ages but we don't know if that sword is sharp. It may be plastic," said Charles Gray, senior vice-president for investments at Prudential Bache in London.

Iraq is preparing celebrations at first light on Tuesday to mark its first crude oil exports since August 1990, when the United Nations reacted to the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait by slapping punitive economic sanctions, including a ban on oil exports.

Under a May 20 agreement, Iraq will be allowed oil exports up to a total $2.0 billion over six months to buy humanitarian goods which it has been unable to import because it has been deprived of vital oil revenue.
No firm buyers have emerged from among the more than 50 oil company executives Baghdad said had flocked to Iraq to conclude term deals.

The first oil is expected to go to neighbouring Turkey, which is already sitting on some 12 million barrels of Iraqi crude oil trapped in the trans-Turkey pipeline when Iraqi troops marched into Kuwait.
Exports to other destinations, particularly the sale of Basrah Light crude to the Far East through the Gulf terminal of Mina al-Bakr, are not expected before January, traders say.

"I think the Iraqis have been a bit too optimistic in expecting to ship on Tuesday. Not one contract has been signed yet. Probably Turkey will be the only ones taking the Iraqi oil as early as Tuesday," said Oystein Berentsen, head of international crude oil trading at Norwegian oil company Statoil .

Five of the world's leading tanker brokerages told Reuters that no company had even expressed interest in hiring tankers to load Iraqi crude at Mina al-Bakr in the south or from Turkey's Mediterranean terminal at Ceyhan.
Iraq, the second biggest oil producer in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) after Saudi Arabia before the Gulf War, produced 3.5 million bpd of crude in July 1990.
According to figures published in the Arab Oil and Gas Journal in 1993, oil exports fell in the eight months to August 1990 to 1.6 million bpd compared with a yearly total of 2.3 million bpd in 1989.

Saudi Arabia used its huge spare capacity to pump volume up to 8.0 million bpd, a rise of nearly 3.0 million bpd which covered the shortfall caused by Iraq's absence and supplied Baghdad's previous clients.

Refinery buyers do not expect to see Iraqi crude oil in their tanks before January at the earliest and they questioned the long-term economics of the Iraqi pricing formula approved by the U.N. Sanctions Committee if compared with Saudi Arabia's Arab Light.

Kirkuk, which is a low-sulphur heavy "sour" crude oil of the type favoured by Mediterranean refineries, is competitive at present if compared with Russia's Urals, widely considered the benchmark in the area.

Iraq has set a discount of $1.55 a barrel to physical Brent compared with a discount of just under 20 cents at present for Urals, which has become expensive of late as volumes have shrunk due to weather and maintenance stoppages at the main Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.

Iraqi crude is expected to displace Russian Urals and Iranian crudes of comparable quality, which too are in short supply Iran's state National Iranian Oil Corp (NIOC) has opted to sell its crude on contract terms rather than on the spot market, traders say.
A senior trader for a European oil company says the threat of resumed Iraqi exports has been weighing on the market for years and is already discounted. He calls them the "phantom Iraqi barrels".
At current prices, Iraq would be able to export no more than 650,000 barrels per day (bpd), which analysts say can easily be absorbed by a tight winter market.

Cold weather prompting high demand for heating fuels as well as the oil industry's recent tendency to keep stocks lean have pushed prices to a near six-year high with Iraq's looming barrels making barely a dent in prices in the weeks leading up to the resumed exports.
"Every day for nearly the past six years, we've been asking when will we see Iraqi oil? What will be talk about now," asked Peter Gignoux, head of the energy desk at Smith Barney.
